title: Rate Limiting
oneLiner: Four ways to cap how many requests a client can make, compared on the same traffic.
keyTakeaway: A fixed window counter is the simplest limiter but can let through twice the limit across a window boundary. Sliding windows fix that, and a token bucket allows short bursts while enforcing an average rate. In a distributed system, the counters usually live in Redis and are updated atomically.
explanation:
A rate limiter caps how many requests a client can make in a period of time, for example 10 requests per 10 seconds. It protects a service from abuse (scrapers, credential stuffing, a buggy client stuck in a retry loop), keeps one customer from using up capacity everyone shares, and controls cost when each request calls something expensive. When a request is over the limit, the service answers with HTTP 429 Too Many Requests and a Retry-After header saying how many seconds to wait, so well behaved clients can back off.

The fixed window counter keeps one counter per client per clock window (0 to 10 seconds, 10 to 20, and so on) and rejects requests once it reaches the limit. It's one number per client and easy to reason about, but it has a known flaw: a client can send the full limit just before a boundary and the full limit again just after, which is twice the limit in a couple of seconds. The burst preset shows it.

The sliding window log stores the timestamp of each allowed request and counts how many fall in the last 10 seconds. It's exact, but it stores one entry per request. The sliding window counter approximates it with two numbers: the current window's count plus the previous window's count weighted by how much of it still overlaps the last 10 seconds. It's nearly as accurate and as cheap as a fixed window, which is why it's a common choice.

The token bucket gives each client a bucket that holds up to N tokens and refills at a steady rate. Each request takes a token; with none left it's rejected. It deliberately allows a burst up to the bucket size and then enforces the refill rate, which matches how real clients behave (a page load fires several requests at once). It's the algorithm behind many API gateways and cloud limits. A leaky bucket is the mirror image: requests join a queue of fixed size that drains at a steady rate, which smooths the output instead of allowing bursts.

Rate limiters usually sit at the edge, in the API gateway (the front-door server every API call passes through) or load balancer, so rejected requests cost almost nothing. The key you limit by matters: per user or per API key is fair for signed-in traffic, per IP address is all you have for anonymous traffic but can punish many users behind one office or mobile carrier address. Many systems apply several limits at once.

With many gateway instances, each one can't keep its own counters, or a client could multiply its limit by the number of instances. The usual answer is a shared store such as Redis, updated with atomic operations (INCR with an expiry for a fixed window, or a small Lua script for a token bucket) so two instances can't both read 9 and both allow the tenth request. That adds a network round trip to every request, so some systems keep approximate local counters and sync them periodically, accepting that a client may briefly exceed the limit. If the store is unreachable, you also have to decide whether to fail open (allow everything) or fail closed (reject everything).
